brief-1.text: The Vantongeren family is a hidden veto holder. The upper runs sit on their farm under a 1987 lease that is 'personal to the co-op', so it cannot be assigned, and operation of those runs cannot effectively be handed to Alderline, without the family's consent. Their interest also changes once a well-funded commercial operator is involved, since the rent has never been raised. A strong reply flags that the family must be brought in and their consent or new lease terms secured before the AGM; otherwise the deal cannot be carried out whatever the members vote.

The roughly 140 lifetime-pass holders make up more than one third of the 410 voting members (140/410 is about 34%), so they can block the two-thirds vote on their own. Their unstated interest is the lifetime pass that Alderline's pass conversion would end, not the abstract 'club feel' debate. A strong reply does this arithmetic, treats them as a blocking bloc, and makes protecting, grandfathering or buying out the lifetime passes part of the deal, rather than accepting the conversion as 'fair'.

The volunteer patrol and ski school hold a hidden veto. Alderline's promise to keep 'all nine employees' covers only paid staff, not the roughly 60 volunteers without whom the hill cannot open (certified patrollers must be on duty). Their unstated interest is the family passes and club role they get in return, which the pass conversion and a commercial operator (who typically cannot rely on unpaid volunteers) put at risk. A strong reply identifies that patrol coverage must be secured explicitly, through pay or preserved arrangements, and notes that the volunteers are also a voting bloc.

Dariusz, and possibly the two other directors who co-signed, have an unstated personal interest: release from their personal guarantee on the $600k operating line. This explains his push for the deal and is a conflict of interest that could discredit the 4-3 board recommendation with members if it is not disclosed. A strong reply names the guarantee as his real interest, calls for disclosure (and recusal where needed), and checks whether the deal actually repays the line or releases the guarantees.

brief-2.text: The Corvane anaesthesia group is a veto holder whose agreement has not been secured. Renewing their contract in June does not commit them to staff new evening and Saturday lists, and their eight anaesthetists already cover labour and delivery and overnight call. Their unstated interests are call burden, fatigue and how the extra lists would be paid. A strong reply treats Corvane's agreement to the extra lists as open and needing negotiation, instead of accepting the user's 'that's settled'.

Sterile Processing is a hidden veto holder. It runs 7am to 6pm on weekdays and reports to Support Services, not to the user, so lists running to 7:30pm and on Saturdays have no instrument reprocessing unless SPD extends its hours and staffing. That needs another director's or VP's agreement and budget. A strong reply flags SPD's hours and reporting line as a blocker to settle before the plan goes to the CEO.

Weekend physiotherapy and ward beds decide whether the extra cases can actually be done. Physio works only Monday to Friday, so Saturday joint patients will not be mobilised until Monday and will stay longer than the usual two nights, on a ward that is already about 95% full. The 450 extra cases also add roughly 900 or more bed-days. A strong reply identifies the physiotherapy department (for weekend cover) and ward or bed management as stakeholders whose agreement and capacity determine whether lists get cancelled.

The nurses' union's unstated interest is getting the suspended OR specialty premium restored and building leverage before April bargaining. Its 'consider' signals a possible pocket veto, with voluntary shifts going unfilled. A strong reply links restoring the premium (or a firm commitment on it) to securing the shifts, rather than assuming time-and-a-half alone will bring volunteers.

brief-3.text: Ilse's earnout is an unstated interest that decides her cooperation. Part of the purchase price depends on her product's revenue through next December, which is exactly the CTO's migration window, so any plan that diverts her engineers or risks churn before December threatens her payout. Her objections are likely to be framed as technical risk. A strong reply names the earnout as her real driver and builds it into the deal (by sequencing the work, adjusting the metric or holding her harmless), rather than treating it as 'standard'.

The Lanternway engineers, especially the two who wrote the routing engine, hold a hidden veto: they can leave. Their retention grants all vest next April, after which nothing holds them, and a plan to rewrite their Elixir engine in Go gives them a reason to go. A strong reply sees that a migration running past April depends on people who can walk away, and proposes new retention, meaningful roles in the new platform, or front-loaded knowledge transfer.

Pellworth Grocers is a hidden veto holder. Moving Lanternway onto Brackwater's cloud adds a new subprocessor, which triggers Pellworth's 120-day notice right, and Pellworth is 31% of Lanternway's revenue (and therefore central to Ilse's earnout). A strong reply flags that the hosting move needs Pellworth engaged early and builds the notice period into the timeline.

Finance has an unstated interest in the roughly $1.2M a year of committed cloud spend that is going unused. That makes moving Lanternway's hosting onto Brackwater's cloud valuable in its own right, whether or not the code is rewritten. A strong reply separates the hosting decision from the rewrite decision, so the CTO's financial case can be met by rehosting the existing services while the contested rewrite is deferred or decided separately. Much of the rewrite fight then turns out to be a false conflict.
